title: This 18-Year-Old Invented a Plastic That Eats Microplastics
summary:
Imagine tiny bits of plastic so small you can't even see them. They're in the ocean, in the soil, in your food, even in the air. They're called microplastics, and they are really, really hard to remove.

But 18-year-old Arya Satheesh from Ireland has a clever idea. She invented something called Eco Purge — a plant-based plastic that breaks down naturally. And here's the cool part: while it decomposes, it also helps break down microplastics that are already polluting the environment.

Arya got interested in microplastics in 2024. She built a water-quality sensor that could find microplastics, but it couldn't remove them. So she decided to fix that.

To make Eco Purge, she needed two natural enzymes. Some companies wanted to sell them to her, but they were way too expensive for a high school student. So she emailed Professor Kevin O'Connor at BiOrbic in Ireland. He got her the enzymes and even let her use a university lab.

By early 2026, she had her first prototype. She tested it in soil, salt water, and fresh water. After six weeks, both the microplastics and the Eco Purge had decomposed.

Her invention won the European regional title at The Earth Prize. She got $12,500 to keep improving it.

"Science isn't just about understanding the world," Arya says. "It's about leaving it better than we found it."
why_it_matters: It shows that a teenager with a good question — and the courage to email a scientist for help — can invent something that helps the whole planet, including the food and water you use every day.

background_read: Microplastics are tiny bits of plastic — smaller than a grain of rice — that break off from bottles, bags and clothes and end up in the ocean, the soil and even the air.
The Earth Prize (a competition that gives money and support to young people around the world with ideas to help the planet) is where Arya's invention won its European regional title.

BiOrbic (a science research centre in Ireland that studies ways to make everyday materials from plants instead of oil) is where Professor Kevin O'Connor works and where Arya was allowed to use a university lab.
Article_Structure: WHO: Arya Satheesh, an 18-year-old inventor from Ireland, helped by Professor Kevin O'Connor at BiOrbic.
WHAT: She invented Eco Purge, a plant-based plastic that breaks down naturally and also helps break down microplastics already polluting the environment.
WHERE: Ireland — she tested the prototype in soil, salt water and fresh water using a university lab.
WHY: Her first sensor could only find microplastics, not remove them, so she built something that could — and it won $12,500 at The Earth Prize.

perspectives.description: Arya proves that you don't need a big company or lots of money; asking for help can open real laboratory doors.
Tests in a small soil or water sample are not the same as cleaning a whole ocean, and it will take years of testing before Eco Purge could be used everywhere.
The story shows a pattern: many young inventors depend on universities, not companies, to get the expensive materials their ideas need.
